title: Evaluating a Generate–Validate–Repair Pipeline for LLM‑based Network Configuration: a Paired, Emulation‑Grounded Study
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired, emulation‑grounded experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) to evaluate whether integrating a deterministic network verifier in a generate–validate–repair (GVR) pipeline reduces unsafe configuration applications from an LLM relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 under shared_initial_candidate semantics (one initial LLM generation per task reused across arms). We ran N=240 paired intent→configuration tasks (144 in‑distribution, 48 distribution‑shift, 48 adversarial). All archived scoring artifacts report safe outcomes for every episode: baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe. The paired risk difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.00; 95% bootstrap percentile CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. Under the preregistered shared_initial_candidate contract the guarded arm could only diverge from baseline if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied; in this run every shared candidate passed validation and no repairs were invoked, producing a degenerate paired contrast. We present the preregistered design, artifact‑grounded execution accounting, exact mapping from estimand to archived analysis artifacts, an artifact‑based failure analysis explaining the null paired outcome, and concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.

sections.introduction:
Automating the translation of high‑level operator intent into concrete device configurations is a central NetOps objective. Large language models (LLMs) and agentic workflows are proposed to produce configuration sequences and operational plans, but conventional token‑level correctness metrics miss ordering, dependency, and invariants required for safe application in live networks. Emulation‑grounded evaluation—where generated configurations are executed in device/simulator images and deterministically scored—exposes semantic failure modes (ordering mistakes, transient invariant violations, protected‑resource touches) not visible in text‑only tests [1].

A widely advocated architectural remedy is the generate–validate–repair (GVR) pattern: an LLM generates a candidate, a deterministic verifier checks semantic invariants, and an automated repair routine rewrites the candidate when violations appear [2,3]. Prior work demonstrates promise for GVR on many syntactic and some semantic faults, but important empirical questions remain about whether deterministic verifiers materially reduce unsafe applications under distribution shift and adversarial prompts and under what experimental contracts those benefits are measurable [2,4].

This paper reports a fully preregistered paired experiment (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01) that measured a single, prespecified estimand: the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline). Execution adhered to shared_initial_candidate semantics (exactly one initial LLM generation per task reused across both arms) so the guarded arm could only change a paired outcome by invoking a validator‑triggered repair. Our contributions are: (1) an artifact‑grounded report of the preregistered paired GVR test and exact mapping from estimand to archived analysis outputs; (2) execution accounting and exact numeric results from the archive (N=240 pairs; baseline_safe=240; guarded_safe=240); and (3) an evidence‑based failure analysis that explains the observed null paired contrast and gives concrete recommendations for future informative GVR evaluations.
sections.related_work:
Recent executable NetOps benchmarks place LLM agents in closed‑loop environments to surface workflow and planning faults rather than only assessing textual fidelity; NetConfArena exemplifies this approach [1]. Research on automatic configuration repair and program repair documents generate–validate patterns and shows that validators often enable high repair coverage for many benchmarked faults, although semantic coverage depends on verifier design and the fault taxonomy [2,4]. Surveys and position papers synthesize agentic architectures, tool augmentation, verifier integration, and uncertainty calibration as promising patterns for operational NetOps automation and safety [3,5]. Engineering precedents (e.g., Batfish) demonstrate the utility of deterministic configuration analysis and incremental verification in network tooling [6].

Our study differs in three experimental choices that matter empirically: (a) a predeclared paired estimand tied to a specific shared_initial_candidate generation contract; (b) emulation‑grounded deterministic scoring for binary safe/unsafe outcomes; and (c) full archival of per‑call traces, validator traces, and analysis artifacts so that every reported number maps precisely to a stored artifact.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimand: The experiment was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01). The primary estimand, paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline, is the absolute paired difference in unsafe_apply rate (guarded − baseline), where unsafe_apply = 1 indicates a final configuration that would cause a semantic safety violation when applied. The analysis executor and its parameters (bootstrap resamples = 10,000; bootstrap seed = 1729) were preregistered and archived.

Design and shared_initial_candidate semantics: We used a paired design with shared_initial_candidate semantics: the adapter produced exactly one initial LLM generation per task and both arms reused that same generation. Under this contract the guarded arm could only change the paired outcome if the shared candidate failed deterministic validation and triggered a repair. This contract was intentionally chosen in the preregistration to reduce model‑call budgets and to produce a directly paired LLM sample; we explicitly treat its causal implications in our analysis.

Task corpus and sampling: The task bank comprised N = 240 distinct intent→configuration tasks generated deterministically. Task composition: in‑distribution 60% (144 tasks), distribution‑shift 20% (48 tasks; novel topologies/vendors), adversarial‑prompt 20% (48 tasks, generated under a fixed adversary seed). Tasks include initial network states, required command sequences, and preserved‑field constraints; representative task manifests and a deterministic task generator were archived.

Model, adapter, and verifier: Execution declared model gpt-5-mini and used adapter family hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and allowed up to one validator‑triggered repair per task per the preregistered adapter contract. Runtime sampling parameters and model‑call metadata were recorded for every model call. The preregistered adapter contract and generation semantics are central to how paired contrasts can arise and are reported explicitly.

Scoring, exclusions, and missingness: The deterministic scorer produced a binary final outcome: safe (0) or unsafe (1), determined by emulator execution and semantic invariant checks recorded in the validator trace. Preregistered exclusions included pairs flagged as 'possible false‑safe' (validator PASS but emulator unsafe outcome) and infra‑failed pairs after allowed retries; sensitivity analyses were specified for these cases. The retry policy allowed up to two infra‑retries; missingness and exclusion counts were archived. No infra failures or 'possible false‑safe' flags occurred in this run.

Statistical analysis: The primary analysis used a paired binary executor producing a paired contingency table, a bootstrap 95% percentile CI (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729), and an exact two‑sided McNemar test on discordant pairs. Secondary planned measures included median repair counts and per‑task model‑call budgets. Multiplicity control was specified for secondary tests; the primary hypothesis was unique.
sections.results:
Execution accounting: The run completed per the preregistered plan. Planned episodes = 480; completed episodes = 480; complete pairs = 240. Provider audit recorded exactly one shared initial generation per task (hosted model call events = 240) and model_calls_used = 240 consistent with shared_initial_candidate semantics. No infra failures or unscorable episodes occurred.

Primary binary outcomes: Every paired episode was scored safe under both arms. Archived condition summaries record baseline successes = 240/240 and guarded successes = 240/240. The paired contingency table is n11 (both safe) = 240; n10 = 0; n01 = 0; n00 = 0. The paired estimator (guarded_unsafe_rate − baseline_unsafe_rate) = 0.00. Bootstrap percentile 95% CI = [0.00, 0.00] (10,000 resamples, seed = 1729). Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0.

Validator and repair activity: No validator‑triggered repairs occurred (repair_attempts = 0 across the run). Representative validator traces show recorded 'validation_before' and 'validation_after' snapshots, difficulty labels ("very_hard"/"extreme"), required command counts, and explicit validator PASS semantics. Because guarded final configurations matched the shared initial candidate for every episode, baseline and guarded outcomes are identical across all subgroups (in‑distribution, shift, adversarial), producing degenerate subgroup contrasts.

Planned sensitivity channels unused: The preregistration included sensitivity analyses that would (a) exclude or treat 'possible false‑safe' flags as unsafe and (b) treat infra‑failed pairs as unsafe. No items were flagged or failed; contamination and missingness summaries are empty.
sections.discussion:
Artifact‑grounded explanation for the null paired contrast: The preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics produced exactly one shared LLM output per task and deterministic_netops_validator_v5 passed every shared candidate. Under the adapter contract the guarded arm could only differ from baseline if the shared candidate failed validation or if a repair was applied; because neither occurred, no discordant pairs were possible and the paired contrast is degenerate. This mechanistic explanation is directly supported by the execution accounting (hosted model calls = 240; model_calls_used = 240), validator traces, and repair logs.

Design tradeoffs and implications: Shared_initial_candidate semantics lowers model‑call cost and guarantees a paired LLM sample, but it also prevents generator variability between arms; therefore empirical demonstration of verifier benefit requires that the shared candidate sometimes fail validation. To detect verifier causal effects in a paired design one should: (A) allow independent initial generations per arm (so the verifier can act on differing generations), (B) increase adversary or generator variability so initial candidates sometimes violate invariants, or (C) enlarge the repair budget and permit iterative repairs until the validator is satisfied. Each choice has operational tradeoffs (cost, latency, interpretability) that must be considered and were signaled in the preregistration.

Statistical interpretation: The realized baseline unsafe_apply rate was 0.0, yielding no power to detect a positive verifier benefit under the chosen generation semantics. The bootstrap CI collapse to [0.00,0.00] reflects the degenerate observed contingency; this is a valid, artifact‑grounded statistical outcome but one that indicates an uninformative contrast under the current design rather than evidence that verifiers are unnecessary in general.

Recommendations (artifact‑grounded): For future paired GVR studies aiming to measure verifier effect size, (1) avoid shared_initial_candidate semantics or include an arm with independent generation; (2) expand adversary protocols beyond a single fixed seed to probe adaptive manipulations; (3) increase repair iterations and instrument repair traces to study repair search behavior; (4) broaden verifier semantic coverage and include cross‑checks between deterministic validator PASS and emulator outcomes to detect possible false‑safe cases.
sections.conclusion: We ran a fully preregistered paired, emulation‑grounded evaluation of a GVR pipeline for LLM‑based network configuration. Observed outcome: every paired episode was safe under both arms (baseline = 240/240 safe; guarded = 240/240 safe), producing a paired difference = 0.00 (95% bootstrap CI [0.00, 0.00]; McNemar p = 1.0). Crucially, the preregistered shared_initial_candidate semantics constrained paired divergence to validator failures or to validator‑triggered repairs; because every shared candidate passed deterministic validation and no repairs occurred, the paired contrast was necessarily degenerate. The archived artifacts include full execution accounting, validator traces, and analysis logs that support these statements and that can be used to design more informative follow‑on experiments that relax shared‑generation constraints, strengthen adversary models, or expand repair budgets.

disclosure_statement: Models and orchestration: Execution used declared model gpt-5-mini via the registered adapter hosted_netops_gvr_v1. The guarded pipeline used deterministic_netops_validator_v5 and permitted up to one validator‑triggered repair per task. Preregistration and autonomy: the study was preregistered (study id study-cand-1-gvr-verifier-adversarial-2026-08-01; preregistration SHA‑256: 3e73ca0dc935a8754bf2dfbe6869ff989c47f1db0d93e2ca34809be8ebf95e26) and executed under the frozen plan after the autonomy lock. Human role and autonomy boundary: prior to the lock the human Research Director selected the topic family and constrained the initial master prompt; all literature search, experiment design, preregistration, execution, analysis, and manuscript drafting occurred autonomously after the lock. Generation semantics: the registered adapter used shared_initial_candidate semantics (one shared initial generation per task reused across both arms); therefore, by design, the guarded vs baseline paired contrast could only differ if the shared initial candidate failed deterministic validation or if a validator‑triggered repair was applied. Execution accounting (high‑level): planned episodes = 480, completed episodes = 480, complete pairs = 240, hosted model call events = 240, model calls used = 240. Immutable master prompt: the initial master prompt is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Archived bundle: execution manifest, per‑call traces, validator traces, task manifests, and analysis artifacts are included in the archived execution bundle and enable reproducibility of the reported estimand mapping; those low‑level artifacts remain in the archive and are not reprinted here. No manual human editing of the technical manuscript content occurred after the autonomy lock.
limitations: Emulator and corpus scope: tasks used a NetConfArena‑style synthetic emulation corpus; external validity to production, multi‑vendor networks and operator workflows is limited.
Single model: a single hosted model (gpt‑5‑mini) was tested; results do not imply generality across models, prompts, or prompting strategies.

Shared_initial_candidate semantics: the paired design used one shared initial generation per task; this prevents generator variability between arms and makes verifier benefit contingent on initial candidate failures.
Adversary bounds: adversarial prompts were generated under a preregistered, fixed adversary protocol and do not represent unconstrained, adaptive adversaries.

Verifier coverage: deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implements a finite set of checks; uncovered semantic fault classes may remain undetected by the verifier, and validator PASS vs emulator outcome mismatches were planned to be flagged and analyzed (none occurred in this run).
